q: There are two main ways of forming chemical bonds between atoms: ionic bonding and covalent bonding.
e: These are the primary mechanisms by which atoms achieve stable electron configurations.

q: There is another important type of chemical bonding, called metallic bonding, which is only found in non-metals.
e: Metallic bonding is only found in metals.

q: The electronic structures of noble gases are very stable and unreactive.
e: They do not need to lose or gain any extra electrons to fill up their outermost shells.

q: In forming a chemical bond, atoms gain, lose or share electrons in such a way to attain the stable electronic structures of the noble gases.
e: This drive for stability is the fundamental reason for chemical bonding.

q: This is to have eight electrons in the outermost shell, which is known as duplet electron configuration.
e: This is to have eight electrons in the outermost shell, which is known as octet electron configuration (Octet Rule).

q: Exception is that helium has only two outer electrons, known as a duplet electron configuration.
e: Helium's first shell is full with just two electrons.

q: An ion is formed when an atom loses or gains electrons, so that it has a charge on it.
e: This charge results from an imbalance between the number of protons and electrons.

q: Metals tend to lose electrons to form negatively charged ions (anions).
e: Metals tend to lose electrons to form positively charged ions (cations).

q: Non-metals tend to gain electrons to form negatively charged ions (anions).
e: Gaining electrons allows non-metals to complete their valence shell.

q: An ionic bond is formed when there is complete transfer of an electron or electrons from one atom to another.
e: This transfer results in the formation of cations and anions.

q: These oppositely charged ions are held together by a force of electrostatic attraction known as ionic bond.
e: This strong attraction forms the basis of ionic compounds.

q: This kind of bond occurs mainly between a metal and a non-metal.
e: The large difference in electronegativity facilitates the transfer of electrons.

q: A covalent bond is formed by the sharing of electrons between two atoms by weak intermolecular forces of attraction.
e: Covalent bonds involve the mutual sharing of electron pairs.

q: Covalent bonds are formed when metal reacts with non-metal.
e: Covalent bonds are formed when non-metal reacts with one another.

q: Ionic compounds do not contain molecules.
e: They consist of aggregates of oppositely charged ions arranged in a lattice.

q: Covalent compounds consist of molecules.
e: Covalent compounds are made of discrete molecular units.

q: Ionic compounds are solids and vaporise easily.
e: Ionic compounds are solids and do not vaporise easily.

q: Simple covalent compounds are gases or volatile liquids (e.g., ammonia, carbon dioxide, ethanol).
e: Weak intermolecular forces allow these compounds to change state easily.

q: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or in aqueous solution.
e: In these states, the ions are free to move and carry an electric current.

q: Most of simple covalent compounds conduct electricity.
e: Most of simple covalent compounds do not conduct electricity.

q: Most ionic compounds have high melting points and high boiling points.
e: Strong electrostatic forces between ions require a lot of energy to break.

q: Simple covalent compounds have low melting points and low boiling points.
e: Only weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome to melt or boil them.

q: Most ionic compounds are soluble in water but not usually soluble in organic solvents such as toluene, ether, benzene, etc.
e: Water's polarity allows it to solvate and separate the ions.

q: Simple covalent compounds are usually insoluble in water and soluble in covalent organic solvents, such as toluene, ether, benzene, etc.
e: Like dissolves like; non-polar covalent compounds dissolve in non-polar solvents.

q: Cation is a positively charged ion.
e: Cations are formed when atoms lose electrons.

q: Anion is a negatively charged ion.
